steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a negative-binomial-randomized gamma Markov process for modeling count time series with heterogeneous overdispersion. Review how count sequences have been modeled (LDSs, rank likelihoods, Poisson gamma dynamical models), explain what they miss, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Count time sequences and why they are hard to model
- Earlier approaches: LDSs, extended rank likelihoods
- Gamma Poisson family / Poisson gamma dynamical models and their advantages
- Gap: heterogeneous overdispersion; graph-structured transitions
- Our contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Count sequences
  - arise in text mining (cite), cell genomic analysis (cite), population movement forecasting (cite)
  - bursty, overdispersed -> not well captured by canonical linear dynamical systems (LDSs) (cite)
- Extended rank likelihood
  - links count observations to latent continuous dynamics (cite)
  - cannot capture bursty dynamics; approximate inference -> scale poorly with high dimensions, e.g. single-cell RNA sequencing (cite)
- Gamma Poisson family
  - recent works model sequential counts with gamma Poisson family (cite)
  - gamma Markov process for continuous dynamics of count sequences (cite); number of latent factors set by gamma process prior, Bayesian non-parametric
  - Poisson gamma dynamical system (cite): transition kernel for how latent dimensions interact
  - tractable, efficient Gibbs sampling via Poisson-Logarithm data augmentation (cite)
  - well-fitted for imputing missing entries, predicting future observations, estimating uncertainties (cite)
- Gap and idea
  - cannot capture heterogeneous overdispersion of latent dynamic processes
  - example: international event data, multiple latent processes changing rapidly with different magnitudes (cite)
  - negative-binomial-randomized gamma Markov chain: more flexible, fast convergence of Gibbs sampling
  - transition dynamics sparse with graph structure -> relational gamma processes (cite)
  - first attempt at latent graph-structured transitions under Poisson gamma dynamical system
- Contributions
  - 1) NBRGMP for heterogeneous overdispersion of latent dimensions
  - 2) relational gamma processes for factor- and graph-structured transitions; more explainable than non-informative priors
  - 3) intractable, but simple, efficient Gibbs sampling via Negative-binomial data augmentation
  - 4) experiments: explainable transition structure; better missing data imputation and future snapshot forecasting than related works

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Count time sequences arise naturally in many domains, like text mining, cell genomic analysis, population movement forecasting, and so on. Modeling count sequences is getting more and more research attention, because real-world count data usually show bursty and overdispersed behaviours, and canonical linear dynamical systems (LDSs) cannot capture these well. Also, some previous works use extended rank likelihood functions to model count time sequences, which link the count observations to latent continuous dynamics. But the extended rank likelihood functions cannot really capture the bursty dynamics that underlie real-world count sequences. They also often need an approximate inference scheme, so they scale poorly for high-dimensional count sequences such as single-cell RNA sequencing data.

Some recent works model sequential count observations with gamma Poisson family distributions. One of them develops a gamma Markov process that captures the continuous dynamics underlying count-valued sequences. In this model the number of latent factors behind high-dimensional count data can be determined appropriately by the gamma process prior, in a Bayesian non-parametric way. Following the success of this work, later work studies a Poisson gamma dynamical system, where a transition kernel is designed to capture how the latent dimensions interact with each other in order to model complicated observed dynamics. Another appealing thing about the Poisson gamma dynamic model is that posterior simulation can be done with a tractable and efficient Gibbs sampling algorithm, using a Poisson-Logarithm data augmentation strategy. So the Poisson gamma dynamic models are particularly well-fitted for imputing missing entries, predicting future unseen observations, and estimating uncertainties.

- Gap and idea
  - cannot capture heterogeneous overdispersion of latent dynamic processes
  - international event data: multiple latent processes, rapid changes, different magnitudes
  - negative-binomial-randomized gamma Markov chain: flexibility + fast Gibbs convergence
  - sparse, graph-structured transitions -> relational gamma processes; first attempt under Poisson gamma dynamical system
- Contributions
  - 1) NBRGMP; 2) relational gamma processes, factor- and graph-structured transitions, more explainable
  - 3) Gibbs sampling via Negative-binomial data augmentation; 4) experiments: explainable structure, imputation and forecasting

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Count time sequences arise naturally in many domains, like text mining, cell genomic analysis, population movement forecasting, and so on. Modeling count sequences is getting more and more research attention, because real-world count data usually show bursty and overdispersed behaviours, and canonical linear dynamical systems (LDSs) cannot capture these well. Also, some previous works use extended rank likelihood functions to model count time sequences, which link the count observations to latent continuous dynamics. But the extended rank likelihood functions cannot really capture the bursty dynamics that underlie real-world count sequences. They also often need an approximate inference scheme, so they scale poorly for high-dimensional count sequences such as single-cell RNA sequencing data.

Some recent works model sequential count observations with gamma Poisson family distributions. One of them develops a gamma Markov process that captures the continuous dynamics underlying count-valued sequences. In this model the number of latent factors behind high-dimensional count data can be determined appropriately by the gamma process prior, in a Bayesian non-parametric way. Following the success of this work, later work studies a Poisson gamma dynamical system, where a transition kernel is designed to capture how the latent dimensions interact with each other in order to model complicated observed dynamics. Another appealing thing about the Poisson gamma dynamic model is that posterior simulation can be done with a tractable and efficient Gibbs sampling algorithm, using a Poisson-Logarithm data augmentation strategy. So the Poisson gamma dynamic models are particularly well-fitted for imputing missing entries, predicting future unseen observations, and estimating uncertainties.

But even with these advantages, these models still cannot capture well the heterogeneous overdispersion effects of the latent dynamic processes behind count observations. For example, international event data usually consists of multiple latent dynamic processes, and these often change rapidly with different magnitudes. To capture this kind of heterogeneous overdispersed behaviour, we develop a negative-binomial-randomized gamma Markov chain structure. It greatly enhances the flexibility of the model, and it also helps the derived Gibbs sampling algorithms converge fast. Also, the transition dynamics behind real-world high-dimensional count data are often sparse and show a certain amount of graph structure. So we propose to learn the graph-structured transition dynamics with relational gamma processes. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to learn latent graph-structured transition dynamics under the Poisson gamma dynamical system.

The main contributions of the paper are: 1) We propose a negative-binomial-randomized gamma Markov process (NBRGMP) to estimate the heterogeneous overdispersion effects of the latent dimensions underlying sequential count observations; 2) We study relational gamma processes thoroughly to learn both factor-structured and graph-structured transition dynamics, which makes the estimated latent structure more explainable compared with transition structure inferred with non-informative priors; 3) The proposed NBRGMP and its factor-structured and graph-structured extensions are intractable, but we develop simple and efficient Gibbs sampling algorithms with Negative-binomial data augmentation strategies to do inference; 4) We conduct extensive experiments to illustrate the explainable transition structure learned by the proposed model. We show that the proposed method performs better than several related works in missing data imputation and future snapshot forecasting.

steps.name: cited_draft
steps.text:

Modeling count sequences is getting more and more research attention, because real-world count data usually show bursty and overdispersed behaviours, and canonical linear dynamical systems (LDSs) [12] cannot capture these well. Also, some previous works use extended rank likelihood functions [13] to model count time sequences, which link the count observations to latent continuous dynamics. But the extended rank likelihood functions cannot really capture the bursty dynamics that underlie real-world count sequences. They also often need an approximate inference scheme, so they scale poorly for high-dimensional count sequences such as single-cell RNA sequencing data [14].

Some recent works [15,16,17,18] model sequential count observations with gamma Poisson family distributions. One of them [15] develops a gamma Markov process that captures the continuous dynamics underlying count-valued sequences. In this model the number of latent factors behind high-dimensional count data can be determined appropriately by the gamma process prior, in a Bayesian non-parametric way. Following the success of this work [15], later work [16] [16] studies a Poisson gamma dynamical system, where a transition kernel is designed to capture how the latent dimensions interact with each other in order to model complicated observed dynamics. Another appealing thing about the Poisson gamma dynamic model is that posterior simulation can be done with a tractable and efficient Gibbs sampling algorithm, using a Poisson-Logarithm data augmentation strategy [19,20]. So the Poisson gamma dynamic models [15,16,18] are particularly well-fitted for imputing missing entries, predicting future unseen observations, and estimating uncertainties.

But even with these advantages, these models still cannot capture well the heterogeneous overdispersion effects of the latent dynamic processes behind count observations. For example, international event data usually consists of multiple latent dynamic processes, and these often change rapidly with different magnitudes [21,22]. To capture this kind of heterogeneous overdispersed behaviour, we develop a negative-binomial-randomized gamma Markov chain structure. It greatly enhances the flexibility of the model, and it also helps the derived Gibbs sampling algorithms converge fast. Also, the transition dynamics behind real-world high-dimensional count data are often sparse and show a certain amount of graph structure. So we propose to learn the graph-structured transition dynamics with relational gamma processes [23]. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to learn latent graph-structured transition dynamics under the Poisson gamma dynamical system.

The main contributions of the paper are: 1) We propose a negative-binomial-randomized gamma Markov process (NBRGMP) to estimate the heterogeneous overdispersion effects of the latent dimensions underlying sequential count observations; 2) We study relational gamma processes thoroughly to learn both factor-structured and graph-structured transition dynamics, which makes the estimated latent structure more explainable compared with transition structure inferred with non-informative priors; 3) The proposed NBRGMP and its factor-structured and graph-structured extensions are intractable, but we develop simple and efficient Gibbs sampling algorithms with Negative-binomial data augmentation strategies to do inference; 4) We conduct extensive experiments to illustrate the explainable transition structure learned by the proposed model. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Count time sequences naturally arise in many domains such as text mining [1,2,3,4,5], cell genomic analysis [6,7,8], population movement forecasting [9,10,11], etc. Modeling count sequences has been drawing increasing research attention because real-world count data usually exhibit bursty and overdispersed behaviours, which cannot be well captured by canonical linear dynamical systems (LDSs) [12]. In addition, some previous works use extended rank likelihood functions [13], which link the count observations to latent continuous dynamics, to model count time sequences. Nonetheless, extended rank likelihood functions cannot faithfully capture the bursty dynamics underlying real-world count sequences. Meanwhile, they often require an approximate inference scheme, and thus scale poorly with high-dimensional count sequences, such as single-cell RNA sequencing data [14]. Notably, some recent works [15,16,17,18] model sequential count observations using gamma Poisson family distributions. More specifically, [15] develops a gamma Markov process to capture the continuous dynamics underlying count-valued sequences. In particular, the number of latent factors behind high-dimensional count data can be appropriately determined by the gamma process prior, in a Bayesian non-parametric manner. Following the success of [15], [16] [16] study a Poisson gamma dynamical system, in which a transition kernel is designed to capture how the latent dimensions interact with each other to model complicated observed dynamics. Another appealing aspect of the Poisson gamma dynamic model is that posterior simulation can be performed with a tractable yet efficient Gibbs sampling algorithm via a Poisson-Logarithm data augmentation strategy [19,20]. Hence, the Poisson gamma dynamic models [15,16,18] are particularly well-suited to impute missing entries, predict future unseen observations and estimate uncertainties.

Despite these advantages, these models still cannot capture well the heterogeneous overdispersion effects of the latent dynamic processes behind count observations. For instance, international event data usually consist of multiple latent dynamic processes, which often change rapidly with different magnitudes [21,22]. To capture such heterogeneous overdispersed behaviours, we develop a negative-binomial-randomized gamma Markov chain structure, which not only greatly enhances model flexibility but also facilitates fast convergence of the derived Gibbs sampling algorithms. Moreover, the transition dynamics behind real-world high-dimensional count data are often sparse and exhibit a certain amount of graph structure. We therefore propose to learn the graph-structured transition dynamics using relational gamma processes [23]. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to learn latent graph-structured transition dynamics under the Poisson gamma dynamical system.

The main contributions of the paper include: 1) A negative-binomial-randomized gamma Markov process (NBRGMP) is proposed to estimate the heterogeneous overdispersion effects of the latent dimensions underlying sequential count observations; 2) Relational gamma processes are thoroughly studied to learn both factor-structured and graph-structured transition dynamics, which makes the estimated latent structure more explainable compared with transition structure inferred using non-informative priors; 3) Although the proposed NBRGMP and its factor-structured and graph-structured extensions are intractable, simple yet efficient Gibbs sampling algorithms are developed via Negative-binomial data augmentation strategies to perform inference; 4) Extensive experiments are conducted to illustrate the explainable transition structure learned by the proposed model. We demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method over several related works in missing data imputation and future snapshot forecasting.
